key_insight: Adding rule-derived labels did not consistently improve prediction over using all budgeted reported labels, and equal-weight augmentation worsened Brier scores across every summarized setting.
clinical_relevance: For antibiotic non-susceptibility prediction, extra weak labels may substantially underestimate risk rather than compensate for scarce reported labels.
method: Studied E. coli urine cultures from Stanford and UT Southwestern using reported-label budgets of 10%, 25%, 50% and 100%.
Compared logistic regression and histogram gradient boosting with reported labels alone versus several rule-label augmentation strategies.
Evaluated five patient-disjoint outer splits using paired patient-cluster bootstrap intervals for Brier-score differences.
evidence_signal: The tuning-selected strategy had a worse median Brier score than the all-budget reported-only baseline in 38 of 40 drug–model–budget summaries.
watch_item: All rule-derived labels were susceptible, and the UT Southwestern rules were not locally validated, limiting confidence in their transferability.
paper_title: Do Rule-Derived Labels Improve Prediction When Reported Labels Are Limited? A Two-Site Machine Learning Study
